extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; educated readers interested in moral philosophy and essays
extracted.subtask_description: An early-modern personal-philosophical essay exploring the nature, virtues, limits, and effects of perfect friendship and the related theme of moderation; aimed at describing and prescribing moral attitudes rather than giving formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness versus obligation in friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is an act of our own choice and voluntary freedom, whereas family relations (father, son, brothers) are friendships imposed by law and natural obligation and therefore contain less of our own voluntary choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts familial ties with true friendship: family bonds are often contrary in humour and lack the spontaneity and voluntary nature of chosen friendship. He emphasizes that voluntary liberty produces affection and friendship more promptly and properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual, constant, and temperate character of friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is 'a general and universal fire, but temperate and equal, a constant established heat, all gentle and smooth, without poignancy or roughness'—a spiritual bond that grows with enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compared with erotic love (described as 'more active, more eager, and more sharp' but fickle and subject to paroxysms), friendship is steady and improves with shared experience; it is spiritual and refines the soul through practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erotic love as bodily, precipitant, and liable to satiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Love (erotic) is 'no other than frantic desire for that which flies from us' and is chiefly bodily, subject to satiety—fruition destroys its motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns that erotic passion is transitory and founded on external beauty; once brought into the terms of friendship (mutual desire achieved), erotic desire often dissipates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect friendship requires judgement and length of time
rubrics_metrics.description: True friendships are 'fortified and confirmed by judgement and the length of time'; they are rare and cannot be confounded with ordinary acquaintances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists on distinguishing perfect friendship from common familiarities: true friendship is tested by deliberation and duration, not by sudden acquaintance or mere utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute concurrence of wills and near-identity of souls
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect friendship consists in an 'absolute concurrence of affections' amounting to 'one soul in two bodies'—friends share wills, thoughts, opinions, goods, honours, wives, children, and lives in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses examples (Laelius & Blosius, Xenophon soldier) to show that such friends would trust each other more readily than themselves and that this unanimity allows instant understanding of motives and intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indivisibility and exclusivity of perfect friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: This highest friendship is indivisible and admits no rivals; a singular friendship 'possesses the whole soul' and 'cannot possibly admit of a rival.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues one cannot truly split this kind of friendship among several: attempting to do so multiplies what is single and undermines the special unity required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of transactional relations among perfect friends
rubrics_metrics.description: In perfect friendship, common concepts of benefit, obligation, acknowledgement, thanks, and entreaty are loathed and banished; friends do not lend or give to one another because their possessions and wills are effectively common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He contrasts this with ordinary friendships which rely on good offices, presents, and reciprocal obligations; in perfect friendship such categories are irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight in enabling the friend to do good (liberality of opportunity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one friend gives a benefit, the liberal action is in affording the friend the opportunity to be useful; the recipient is the man who obliges his friend by allowing him to confer the benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne illustrates with Diogenes' remark about re-demanding money of friends and the Eudamidas will story, showing the moral value is in permitting the friend to exercise generosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between instrumental/functional relationships and friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Relationships that hold by a single end (physician, lawyer, servant) are judged by utility for that end (diligence, ability), not by broader moral qualities (religion, chastity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises evaluating people according to the role they serve: e.g., don't inquire about a footman's chastity, but about his diligence; do not conflate professional or instrumental ties with the moral unity of true friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-appropriate preferences in ordinary acquaintance
rubrics_metrics.description: One should prefer different qualities in different contexts: table-talk favors the pleasant and witty over the grave and learned; in bed, beauty before goodness; in common discourse, the ablest speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is practical advice on choosing companions for specific occasions and acknowledges that ordinary social relations have varying standards depending on function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution and prudence in ordinary friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary friendships require walking 'with bridle in your hand, with prudence and circumspection' because the knot is not so sure; one should adopt the precept 'Love him so as if you were one day to hate him,' i.e., retain some reserve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recommends self-protection and measured expectations in commonplace friendships, citing Aristotle's aphorism 'O my friends, there is no friend.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The singular value and irreplaceability of a true friend
rubrics_metrics.description: The possession of a true friend surpasses other pleasures; the loss of such a friend can render life languishing and make other pleasures aggravate the grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses personal testimony and classical quotations to show how central and formative a single perfect friendship can be to one's life and happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding excess in virtue — the doctrine of moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue itself can be carried to excess and become vicious; 'The wise man is no longer wise, the just man no longer just, if he seek to carry his love for wisdom or virtue beyond that which is necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne endorses a measured approach: excessive zeal—even for good—astonishes and harms; he cites scripture (St. Paul) and classical sources to argue for sober wisdom and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance philosophical inquiry with practical life
rubrics_metrics.description: The extremity of philosophy is hurtful: taken to excess it can make a man 'brutish and vicious,' contemptuous of religion and common laws, unfit for public administration and human pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He warns that excessive subtlety enslaves natural freedom and leads away from the fair and beaten way nature traces; philosophy should be moderated to remain useful and sociable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance in conjugal pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Marital pleasures are lawful but must be curbed: 'the pleasure we extract from [marriage] should be a sober and serious delight, and mixed with a certain kind of gravity'; immoderate licentiousness within marriage is reproachable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne counsels husbands against indulging immodest and debauched postures and tricks suggested by first ardour; he appeals to theological and cultural authorities (St. Thomas, Plato, various customs) as background for moderation in conjugal conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control as mark of best-taught individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Those best taught in divinity and philosophy are 'best able to control and curb their own liberty'; ability to govern one's liberty is a sign of good instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes that theology and philosophy claim jurisdiction over private actions, and he aligns good teaching with the capacity for self-restraint rather than mere exhibition of knowledge or fervor.
